results.construction: Points mode, range [-6,6]: tap x=-3 and x=3. Denominator x^2-9=0 gives x=±3; both are whole numbers inside the range, and the numerator is nonzero at both, so there is no cancellation. Reachable.

predicates.why: A student who sets the numerator to zero marks only x=1. That value is not in {-3,3}, so extra-values fires. This is the most natural reason to mark 1 for this question, so the diagnosis fits.

A student who solves x^2=9 and keeps only x=3 marks {3} and misses -3, so missed-values fires. This is the typical one-root error. The predicate would also fire for the numerator-zero student, but this construction is exactly what the one-root misconception produces.

results.construction: Points mode, range [-6,6]: tap -2 and 2. Both are whole numbers inside the range, and there are 2 targets (within the 1–4 limit).

predicates.why: It fires when only part of the set is marked, for example just 2, or just -2. A student holding the one-root-only-denominator misconception would mark only the positive root, 2, and that does trigger missed-values. But missed-values also fires for any partial answer, such as marking only -2, or marking one root plus a stray value. It is a generic partial-set signal, so it is not specific to this misconception. The 'when in doubt, false' rule applies.

It fires when the student marks values outside the answer set. A student who sets the numerator to zero marks x=-1, and -1 is an extra value, so the predicate would fire. But that student would also leave out -2 and 2, so the construction is only a partial match for the excludes-numerator-zeroes error. The predicate would also fire for many other errors, such as marking 4 or 0. It is not specific to this misconception.

results.construction: Points mode, range [-6,6]: tap x=-3 and x=2 on the number line (set {-3,2}); both are whole numbers inside the range, 2 targets.

predicates.why: Marking only one of {-3,2} (e.g. just x=2 or just x=-3) leaves part of the answer set unmarked, which is exactly the student who finds one zero of the denominator and stops. Mode is points, so the predicate can fire. Caveat: a student marking only one value might also have sign confusion, but marking a strict subset fits the 'stopped after one factor' misconception well.

results.construction: Points mode, range [-6,6]; tap -1 and 4 (denominator zeros of (x+1)(x-4)). Both are whole numbers within range, 2 targets within 1–4 limit.

predicates.why: Fires when the student marks only a subset, e.g. just -1 or just 4 (or neither fully). A student who finds one breaking value and stops marks exactly one of the two, which is the described misconception. Could also fire from carelessness, but the single-zero pattern is the main cause.

results.construction: Denominator (x-5)(x+2) is zero at x=5 and x=-2. On range [-6,6], tap -2 and 5 in points mode. Both are whole numbers inside the range, 2 targets, so valid.

predicates.why: Fires when the marked set is a proper subset of {-2,5}, e.g. only 5 or only -2. That is what a student does who finds one value that makes the denominator zero and stops, or who handles only one factor. The set-grading predicate lists missed-values for points mode, so it can fire. Other causes are possible, such as a mis-tap, but one-factor-only is the dominant reason.
